joineRML and the broom package

Alessandro Gasparini and Graeme L. Hickey

2026-11-24

Source: vignettes/joineRML-tidy.Rmd
joineRML-tidy.Rmd

Introduction

joineRML provides three broom-compatible methods for fitted joint models:

  • tidy() returns coefficient estimates, standard errors, and optional confidence intervals.
  • augment() adds longitudinal fitted values and residuals to the original observations.
  • glance() returns a one-row summary of model fit and sample sizes.

These methods support plots, model comparisons, and tables. They can be used without loading broom; if broom is loaded, the same joineRML methods are used regardless of package loading order. Unsupported arguments cause an error rather than being silently ignored.

Example

We use the sample example from the introductory vignette to joineRML using the heart valve data.

vignette("joineRML", package = "joineRML")
help("heart.valve", package = "joineRML")

We analyse only the records with case-complete data for heart valve gradient (grad) and left ventricular mass index (lvmi):

data(heart.valve)
hvd <- heart.valve[!is.na(heart.valve$grad) & !is.na(heart.valve$lvmi), ]

Further to that, we only select the first 50 individuals to speed up these examples:

hvd <- hvd[hvd$num <= 50, ]
set.seed(12345)
fit <- mjoint(
  formLongFixed = list(
    "grad" = log.grad ~ time + sex + hs,
    "lvmi" = log.lvmi ~ time + sex
  ),
  formLongRandom = list(
    "grad" = ~ 1 | num,
    "lvmi" = ~ time | num
  ),
  formSurv = Surv(fuyrs, status) ~ age,
  data = list(hvd, hvd),
  timeVar = "time"
)
## Running multivariate LMM EM algorithm to establish initial parameters...
## Finished multivariate LMM EM algorithm...
## EM algorithm has converged!
## Calculating post model fit statistics...

tidy method

The tidy method returns a tidy dataset with model estimates.

tidy(fit)
## # A tibble: 3 × 8
##   term    estimate std.error statistic p.value component outcome effect     
##   <chr>      <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl> <chr>     <chr>   <chr>      
## 1 age        0.137    0.0665     2.05   0.0401 survival  event   fixed      
## 2 gamma_1    2.85     3.73       0.763  0.446  survival  grad    association
## 3 gamma_2    3.68     3.45       1.07   0.286  survival  lvmi    association

By default the tidy method returns the estimated coefficients for the survival component of the joint model; however, it is possible to extract each component by setting the component argument:

tidy(fit, component = "longitudinal")
## # A tibble: 7 × 8
##   term            estimate std.error statistic  p.value component outcome effect
##   <chr>              <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl> <chr>     <chr>   <chr> 
## 1 (Intercept)_1    2.52       0.165     15.2   1.70e-52 longitud… grad    fixed 
## 2 time_1           0.00951    0.0307     0.310 7.56e- 1 longitud… grad    fixed 
## 3 sex_1            0.0344     0.231      0.149 8.82e- 1 longitud… grad    fixed 
## 4 hsStentless va…  0.0825     0.199      0.415 6.78e- 1 longitud… grad    fixed 
## 5 (Intercept)_2    4.99       0.0818    61.1   0        longitud… lvmi    fixed 
## 6 time_2           0.0258     0.0129     2.00  4.58e- 2 longitud… lvmi    fixed 
## 7 sex_2           -0.197      0.211     -0.934 3.50e- 1 longitud… lvmi    fixed

Use component = "all" to combine both components. The component, outcome, and effect columns distinguish longitudinal fixed effects, survival covariates, and latent association coefficients. Outcome labels use the names supplied in formLongFixed, or the response expressions if the list was unnamed. Existing coefficient names are retained.

tidy(fit, component = "all", conf.int = TRUE)
## # A tibble: 10 × 10
##    term       estimate std.error statistic  p.value conf.low conf.high component
##    <chr>         <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>    
##  1 (Intercep…  2.52       0.165     15.2   1.70e-52  2.20e+0    2.85   longitud…
##  2 time_1      0.00951    0.0307     0.310 7.56e- 1 -5.06e-2    0.0696 longitud…
##  3 sex_1       0.0344     0.231      0.149 8.82e- 1 -4.19e-1    0.488  longitud…
##  4 hsStentle…  0.0825     0.199      0.415 6.78e- 1 -3.08e-1    0.473  longitud…
##  5 (Intercep…  4.99       0.0818    61.1   0         4.83e+0    5.15   longitud…
##  6 time_2      0.0258     0.0129     2.00  4.58e- 2  4.84e-4    0.0512 longitud…
##  7 sex_2      -0.197      0.211     -0.934 3.50e- 1 -6.09e-1    0.216  longitud…
##  8 age         0.137      0.0665     2.05  4.01e- 2  6.17e-3    0.267  survival 
##  9 gamma_1     2.85       3.73       0.763 4.46e- 1 -4.47e+0   10.2    survival 
## 10 gamma_2     3.68       3.45       1.07  2.86e- 1 -3.08e+0   10.4    survival 
## # ℹ 2 more variables: outcome <chr>, effect <chr>

It is also possible to require confidence intervals to be calculated by setting conf.int = TRUE, and modify the confidence level by setting the conf.level argument:

tidy(fit, conf.int = TRUE)
## # A tibble: 3 × 10
##   term    estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low conf.high component
##   <chr>      <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>    
## 1 age        0.137    0.0665     2.05   0.0401  0.00617     0.267 survival 
## 2 gamma_1    2.85     3.73       0.763  0.446  -4.47       10.2   survival 
## 3 gamma_2    3.68     3.45       1.07   0.286  -3.08       10.4   survival 
## # ℹ 2 more variables: outcome <chr>, effect <chr>
tidy(fit, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.99)
## # A tibble: 3 × 10
##   term    estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low conf.high component
##   <chr>      <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>    
## 1 age        0.137    0.0665     2.05   0.0401  -0.0348     0.308 survival 
## 2 gamma_1    2.85     3.73       0.763  0.446   -6.77      12.5   survival 
## 3 gamma_2    3.68     3.45       1.07   0.286   -5.20      12.6   survival 
## # ℹ 2 more variables: outcome <chr>, effect <chr>

For the survival component, exponentiate = TRUE returns exponentiated estimates and confidence limits. Standard errors and test statistics remain on the log-hazard scale. For a baseline covariate, the exponentiated coefficient is its conditional hazard ratio per unit increase, holding other terms fixed. For an association coefficient, the unit refers to its latent process rather than the observed marker. Exponentiation is rejected for longitudinal or combined output.

tidy(fit, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE)
## # A tibble: 3 × 10
##   term    estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low conf.high component
##   <chr>      <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>    
## 1 age         1.15    0.0665     2.05   0.0401   1.01        1.31 survival 
## 2 gamma_1    17.2     3.73       0.763  0.446    0.0115  25945.   survival 
## 3 gamma_2    39.7     3.45       1.07   0.286    0.0460  34187.   survival 
## # ℹ 2 more variables: outcome <chr>, effect <chr>

The standard errors reported by default are based on the empirical information matrix, as in mjoint. It is of course possible to use bootstrapped standard errors as follows:

bSE <- bootSE(fit, 
              nboot = 100, 
              safe.boot = TRUE, 
              progress = FALSE,
              ncores = 1L)
tidy(fit, bootSE = bSE, conf.int = TRUE)

The spelling boot_se = bSE, used by broom, is also accepted. Supply only one of bootSE and boot_se. Both use the supplied bootstrap standard errors in normal-approximation confidence intervals.

The results of this example are not included as it would take too long to run for CRAN.

The tidy method is useful for custom plotting (e.g. forest plots) of results from joineRML models, all in a tidy framework:

library(ggplot2)
out <- tidy(fit, conf.int = TRUE)
ggplot(out, aes(x = term, y = estimate, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar()

augment method

The augment method returns a dataset with added predictions from the joint model. In particular, population-level and individual-level fitted values and residuals are added to the data frame returned by the method:

preds <- augment(fit)
head(preds[, c("num", "log.grad", ".fitted_grad_0", ".fitted_grad_1", ".resid_grad_0", ".resid_grad_1")])
## # A tibble: 6 × 6
##   num   log.grad .fitted_grad_0 .fitted_grad_1 .resid_grad_0 .resid_grad_1
##   <fct>    <dbl>          <dbl>          <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>
## 1 1         2.30           2.60           2.42        -0.302        -0.113
## 2 1         2.30           2.64           2.45        -0.337        -0.148
## 3 1         2.30           2.65           2.46        -0.346        -0.158
## 4 10        2.20           2.56           2.40        -0.364        -0.201
## 5 10        2.20           2.60           2.43        -0.398        -0.236
## 6 11        3.69           2.61           2.65         1.08          1.04
head(preds[, c("num", "log.lvmi", ".fitted_lvmi_0", ".fitted_lvmi_1", ".resid_lvmi_0", ".resid_lvmi_1")])
## # A tibble: 6 × 6
##   num   log.lvmi .fitted_lvmi_0 .fitted_lvmi_1 .resid_lvmi_0 .resid_lvmi_1
##   <fct>    <dbl>          <dbl>          <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>
## 1 1         4.78           4.99           4.75       -0.214         0.0292
## 2 1         4.78           5.09           4.87       -0.309        -0.0867
## 3 1         4.92           5.11           4.90       -0.190         0.0267
## 4 10        5.14           5.10           5.06        0.0377        0.0723
## 5 10        5.13           5.19           5.17       -0.0635       -0.0397
## 6 11        5.03           5.00           5.05        0.0303       -0.0263

By default, rows follow the fitted subject-time order. Supplying data = hvd returns the original observations in that dataset’s order, matched by subject ID and measurement time. All original columns must be present and unchanged; subject-time pairs must be unique if reordering is needed. Outcomes with different observation schedules cannot be combined into this single data frame. augment() does not accept newdata; use dynLong() or dynSurv() for dynamic predictions.

We can plot the resulting predictions for four distinct individuals:

out <- preds[preds$num %in% c(26, 36, 227, 244), ]
ggplot(out, aes(x = time, colour = num)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = log.grad, linetype = "Measured")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = .fitted_grad_1, linetype = "Fitted")) +
  labs(linetype = "Type", colour = "ID", y = "Aortic gradient")

glance method

The glance method allows extracting summary statistics from the joint model:

glance(fit)
## # A tibble: 1 × 11
##   sigma_1 sigma_2   AIC   BIC logLik  nobs nevent  npar converged
##     <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl> <int>  <dbl> <dbl> <lgl>    
## 1   0.517   0.158  342.  374.  -153.    43      8    18 TRUE     
## # ℹ 2 more variables: nobs_longitudinal_1 <int>, nobs_longitudinal_2 <int>

nobs is the number of subjects, agreeing with nobs(fit) and the sample size used by BIC. nevent counts observed events, and nobs_longitudinal_1, nobs_longitudinal_2, and so on count measurements for each outcome in formula order. npar is the parameter count used by AIC and BIC, excluding baseline hazard increments. converged records whether the fitting criterion was met. These summaries are available even when post-fit standard errors were not requested.

The sigma_1, sigma_2, and subsequent columns contain residual standard deviations, agreeing with sigma(fit) and summary(fit)$sigma. The stored coef(fit)$sigma2 values are variances. For example, a residual variance of 0.25 corresponds to a residual standard deviation of 0.5. Bootstrap residual estimates and confidence intervals remain on the variance scale, and bootSE() reports standard errors of the variance estimates.

sigma(fit)                  # Residual standard deviations, named by outcome
##      grad      lvmi 
## 0.5171520 0.1581865
coef(fit)$sigma2             # Residual variances
##   sigma2_1   sigma2_2 
## 0.26744623 0.02502296

This allows comparing competing models easily. Say for instance that we fit a second model with only random intercepts:

set.seed(67890)
fit2 <- mjoint(
  formLongFixed = list(
    "grad" = log.grad ~ time + sex + hs,
    "lvmi" = log.lvmi ~ time + sex
  ),
  formLongRandom = list(
    "grad" = ~ 1 | num,
    "lvmi" = ~ 1 | num
  ),
  formSurv = Surv(fuyrs, status) ~ age,
  data = list(hvd, hvd),
  timeVar = "time"
)
## Running multivariate LMM EM algorithm to establish initial parameters...
## Finished multivariate LMM EM algorithm...
## EM algorithm has converged!
## Calculating post model fit statistics...

We can go ahead and compare the models in terms of AIC and BIC:

glance(fit)
## # A tibble: 1 × 11
##   sigma_1 sigma_2   AIC   BIC logLik  nobs nevent  npar converged
##     <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl> <int>  <dbl> <dbl> <lgl>    
## 1   0.517   0.158  342.  374.  -153.    43      8    18 TRUE     
## # ℹ 2 more variables: nobs_longitudinal_1 <int>, nobs_longitudinal_2 <int>
glance(fit2)
## # A tibble: 1 × 11
##   sigma_1 sigma_2   AIC   BIC logLik  nobs nevent  npar converged
##     <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl> <int>  <dbl> <dbl> <lgl>    
## 1   0.515   0.173  342.  369.  -156.    43      8    15 TRUE     
## # ℹ 2 more variables: nobs_longitudinal_1 <int>, nobs_longitudinal_2 <int>

Compare AIC and BIC only for models fitted to the same observations, and check convergence before interpreting the comparison.

Extracting a model component

The following methods describe a selected longitudinal fixed-effects model. Coefficient names and covariance-matrix names agree with its design columns:

nobs(fit)
## [1] 43
terms(fit, process = "Longitudinal", k = 2)
## log.lvmi ~ time + sex
## attr(,"variables")
## list(log.lvmi, time, sex)
## attr(,"factors")
##          time sex
## log.lvmi    0   0
## time        1   0
## sex         0   1
## attr(,"term.labels")
## [1] "time" "sex" 
## attr(,"order")
## [1] 1 1
## attr(,"intercept")
## [1] 1
## attr(,"response")
## [1] 1
## attr(,".Environment")
## <environment: R_GlobalEnv>
## attr(,"predvars")
## list(log.lvmi, time, sex)
## attr(,"dataClasses")
##  log.lvmi      time       sex 
## "numeric" "numeric" "numeric"
head(model.frame(fit, process = "Longitudinal", k = 2))
##    log.lvmi      time sex
## 1  4.778955 0.0109589   0
## 2  4.778955 3.6794520   0
## 3  4.924569 4.6958900   0
## 43 5.137150 4.1205480   0
## 44 5.129366 7.7342470   0
## 45 5.027165 0.1534247   0
head(model.matrix(fit, process = "Longitudinal", k = 2))
##    (Intercept)      time sex
## 1            1 0.0109589   0
## 2            1 3.6794520   0
## 3            1 4.6958900   0
## 43           1 4.1205480   0
## 44           1 7.7342470   0
## 45           1 0.1534247   0
coef(fit, process = "Longitudinal", k = 2)
## (Intercept)        time         sex 
##  4.99293606  0.02584591 -0.19671311
vcov(fit, process = "Longitudinal", k = 2)
##               (Intercept)          time           sex
## (Intercept)  0.0066862346 -0.0002348949 -0.0015748512
## time        -0.0002348949  0.0001674460 -0.0005463331
## sex         -0.0015748512 -0.0005463331  0.0443159100

Model frames contain evaluated terms, including transformations. Fitted contrasts are retained, so extraction is unaffected by subsequent changes to the original dataset or R’s contrast options. These methods extract the fitted observations and do not accept new data.

Use process = "Event" for the survival formula. Its design matrix contains baseline covariates, without an intercept or latent association columns. Event coefficient and covariance selections include both baseline covariates and association coefficients:

head(model.matrix(fit, process = "Event"))
##         age
## 1  75.06027
## 43 72.12329
## 45 70.56712
## 51 50.97534
## 56 69.94247
## 62 72.30685
coef(fit, process = "Event")
##       age   gamma_1   gamma_2 
## 0.1365893 2.8471790 3.6800987
vcov(fit, process = "Event")
##                  age     gamma_1     gamma_2
## age      0.004427543 -0.03287174 -0.03879102
## gamma_1 -0.032871736 13.93535531 -6.12718700
## gamma_2 -0.038791016 -6.12718700 11.89414499

The default coef(fit) still returns the original parameter list, and vcov(fit) still returns the covariance matrix for all main parameters. Selecting longitudinal coefficients without k returns all outcomes, retaining their numbered suffixes. Covariance extraction requires available post-fit standard errors.

Tables with modelsummary and gtsummary

These optional packages can format the extracted results. Supplying the tidied estimates explicitly makes the selected component and reported sample sizes clear.

For modelsummary, combine tidy() and glance() in a modelsummary_list object:

table_model <- structure(
  list(tidy = tidy(fit, conf.int = TRUE), glance = glance(fit)),
  class = "modelsummary_list"
)
modelsummary::modelsummary(
  list("Joint model" = table_model),
  gof_map = data.frame(
    raw = c("nobs", "nevent", "AIC", "BIC"),
    clean = c("Subjects", "Events", "AIC", "BIC"),
    fmt = c(0, 0, 1, 1)
  ),
  output = "markdown"
)
Joint model
age 0.137
(0.067)
gamma_1 2.847
(3.733)
gamma_2 3.680
(3.449)
Subjects 43
Events 8
AIC 342.4
BIC 374.1

For gtsummary, format the combined coefficient table directly. This retains all outcome labels and avoids treating the joint model as a single regression formula:

table_data <- tidy(fit, component = "all", conf.int = TRUE)
table_data <- table_data[c("component", "outcome", "term", "estimate",
                           "conf.low", "conf.high", "p.value")]
gtsummary::as_gtsummary(table_data) |>
  gtsummary::modify_header(
    component = "Component", outcome = "Outcome", term = "Term",
    estimate = "Estimate", conf.low = "Lower 95% CI",
    conf.high = "Upper 95% CI", p.value = "p-value"
  ) |>
  gtsummary::modify_fmt_fun(
    c(estimate, conf.low, conf.high) ~ gtsummary::label_style_number(digits = 3),
    p.value ~ gtsummary::label_style_pvalue(digits = 3)
  )
Component Outcome Term Estimate Lower 95% CI Upper 95% CI p-value
longitudinal grad (Intercept)_1 2.522 2.198 2.846 <0.001
longitudinal grad time_1 0.010 -0.051 0.070 0.756
longitudinal grad sex_1 0.034 -0.419 0.488 0.882
longitudinal grad hsStentless valve_1 0.083 -0.308 0.473 0.678
longitudinal lvmi (Intercept)_2 4.993 4.833 5.153 <0.001
longitudinal lvmi time_2 0.026 0.000 0.051 0.046
longitudinal lvmi sex_2 -0.197 -0.609 0.216 0.350
survival event age 0.137 0.006 0.267 0.040
survival grad gamma_1 2.847 -4.469 10.164 0.446
survival lvmi gamma_2 3.680 -3.079 10.440 0.286
